cards.title: Authority Persuasion in Ecommerce: Defense Checklist
cards.summary: Two questions—is this a true expert, and how truthful is the expert here—help shoppers and operators resist automatic deference triggered by titles, uniforms and trappings.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to follow an 'expert' recommendation that affects merchandising, pricing, fulfillment or store policy, or when auditing your own site's claims for credibility.
steps: Because authority prompts automatic compliance, Cialdini argues, we should not resist all guidance—most experts do know their field. Instead, calibrate: ask whether the authority is a genuine expert on this specific topic.
Ask a second question: how truthful is this expert likely to be here? Check whether they benefit from your compliance. Cialdini says we are swayed more by experts who seem impartial.

Watch for the tactic of 'arguing against self-interest' on a minor point (e.g., 'Avis: we're number two, but we try harder'; 'Listerine, the taste you hate three times a day') used to establish honesty before pushing a bigger claim.

For an ecommerce store: apply this to your own expert claims. If you cite 'dermatologist tested', a certification, or a professional endorsement, make the credential specific and relevant to the product, not just an authority symbol.
Avoid using actors or unrelated celebrities to imply medical or technical authority—Cialdini calls this using an empty title as a symbol.
When deciding whether to follow a vendor, consultant, platform or supplier recommendation, check credentials' relevance to your specific problem and how the recommender stands to gain.
caveats: Cialdini's own examples are TV ads and personal anecdotes; the transfer of the two-question check to ecommerce settings is a suggested application, not a tested store outcome.
Blind obedience is not all bad—authority shortcuts often work; the check is for the exceptions.

cards.title: Recognize When Authority Symbols Replace Real Credentials
cards.summary: Titles, clothing and expensive trappings trigger compliance even without genuine expertise, so shoppers and operators should separate symbol from substance.
cards.use_when: Merchandising or creating content where authority-like signals (badges, uniforms, expert imagery, luxury cues) are used, and when assessing competitor claims or negotiating with suppliers.
steps: Know the three symbol categories: titles (e.g., 'professor', 'Doctor'), clothing (uniforms, business suits), and trappings (jewelry, prestige cars).

Cialdini cites studies: in one, pedestrians followed a jaywalker 3.5 times more often when he wore a business suit than work clothes, though following crossing behavior is a demonstration, not ecommerce evidence.
In Bickman's guard-uniform experiment, nearly all pedestrians complied when the requester wore the uniform versus fewer than half in street clothes.
For your store, use these as hypotheses, not universal claims: test whether expert badges, professional imagery or verified credentials change add-to-cart or conversion.
Audit your own claims: if a testimonial or badge relies on a title with no relevance to the product category, replace it with a relevant credential or remove it.
caveats: The cited studies measure street compliance, not purchase behavior; per the source these effects are examples, not validated ecommerce lift.
Cialdini notes people underestimate authority's influence, so intuition and customer surveys may under-report the effect.

cards.title: Use Scarcity Framing to Increase Willingness to Buy
cards.summary: Framing offers around potential loss rather than gain tends to motivate more action, because scarcity makes the same item feel more valuable.
cards.use_when: Writing product page copy, email subject lines or ad creative for a limited stock, seasonal or discontinued item.
steps: Present the offer in loss terms: state what the customer stands to lose by not acting, not only what they gain. Cialdini cites health researchers: self-exam pamphlets were more successful when framed as losses than as equal gains.
Another cited example is homeowners more likely to insulate when told how much money they could lose than how much they could save.
For your PDP or ad: instead of 'save 20%', consider stating the specific loss ('this price is gone at midnight') when the constraint is real.
Pair with the actual limiting factor: limited number, end of production, or a deadline. Cialdini notes limited-number information was sometimes true and sometimes false among practitioners.
Test loss-framed against gain-framed variants rather than assuming one wins.
caveats: The insulation and health-pamphlet findings are not ecommerce conversion studies; treat them as framing hypotheses.
Using false scarcity or fake deadlines risks eroding trust and can violate consumer protection rules—verify claims are truthful.

cards.title: Limited-Number Technique and the Commit-While-Scarcest Play
cards.summary: Limited inventory messages raise perceived value, and one advanced application asks customers to commit when availability looks lowest.
cards.use_when: Launching limited drops, managing low-stock SKUs, or designing recovery messaging for out-of-stock items.
steps: Use the straightforward limited-number statement: inform the customer the product is in short supply and may not last, e.g., 'only two unsold corner lots remain'.
Cialdini describes a store version: a salesperson tells interested buyers the last unit was just sold, letting disappointment raise perceived value.
Then, before checking for more stock, the salesperson asks the customers to commit to buying the model at that price if it can be found—so commitment is secured while the item looks least available.
This works because the scarcity principle pushes customers to commit while an item looks least available and therefore most desirable.
For ecommerce: apply honestly via low-stock indicators and waitlist or back-in-stock flows that capture the commitment, and notify promptly.
Cialdini notes that once found, the item becomes less attractive again, but the earlier commitment often still holds.
caveats: The source describes this tactic from a sales-floor investigation where stock information could be manipulated; telling customers an item is sold out when it is not is deceptive and should not be copied.

Its effectiveness depends on the initial interest cue (browsing, instruction-booklet reading) that the source says the salesperson used to judge intent; for online stores the analogue is behavioral signals such as repeat views.

cards.title: Deadline Pressure: Shrinking Opportunity Window
cards.summary: Deadlines make people act on opportunities they otherwise would ignore, because the time to get something is running out.
cards.use_when: Planning flash sales, launch windows, enrollment periods for subscriptions or membership tiers, or limited-time bundles.
steps: Cialdini's personal example: he only wanted to tour the Mormon temple's restricted section after learning it would be open to non-members for only several days—the shrinking window, not interest in the temple, drove the urge.
Apply the same logic to store promotions: a clear end time can generate interest where none existed before.
Merchandisers publicize customer deadlines; the source shows newspaper ad examples of concentrated deadline appeals, e.g. in movie advertising.
Pair a deadline with a concrete cutoff ('offer ends Friday 11:59pm'), and honor it when the clock runs out.
Test deadline-driven vs. evergreen offers, especially for considered purchases, and measure incremental revenue against margin given away.
caveats: Cialdini's examples come from advertising and personal experience rather than measured ecommerce results.
Deadlines must reflect real constraints; fake scarcity or restocked extensions train customers to distrust your deadlines.

cards.title: Scarcity Raises Perceived Value, Even for Flawed Items
cards.summary: Rare or becoming-rare items are judged more valuable, and even flaws become prized when tied to scarcity.
cards.use_when: Positioning limited editions, discontinued lines, archive or vintage inventory, and setting prices for rare stock.
steps: Cialdini cites the 'precious mistake': a blurred stamp or double-struck coin can be among the most valued collectibles—imperfections become prized when they bring abiding scarcity.
For ecommerce, treat scarcity as a positioning variable: limited runs, region- or season-limited prints, and last-of-line stock can justify a premium.
Identify which of your SKUs are genuinely scarce—made-once, discontinued, small-batch—and feature that fact in merchandising rather than discounting them like commodity stock.
Be specific about the basis of scarcity (edition size, run ended, no restock) so the claim is verifiable.
Do not invent rarity for ordinary items; the principle works when the constraint is plausible and consistent.
caveats: The collectibles evidence is auction/collector anecdote from the source, not ecommerce pricing data.
Scarcity pricing can backfire if customers can easily find the same goods elsewhere cheaper.

cards.title: Detecting the Self-Interest Disguise in Vendor and Partner Pitches
cards.summary: When someone argues against their own interest on a small point, it can be a credibility move designed to make a bigger ask land.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with suppliers, agencies, platforms or marketplace partners, and when writing your own sales or upsell copy.
steps: Cialdini describes Vincent the waiter: for large parties, he warned that a chosen dish 'isn't as good tonight', then recommended two dishes about fifty cents cheaper.

He warned that a chosen dish wasn't as good that night and recommended two dishes about fifty cents cheaper. This made him look knowledgeable and honest, and built a felt obligation to reciprocate. He then suggested costly wines and desserts, and his tip percentage and bill size both rose.

Cialdini's Reader's Report example: a used-car dealer told a seller to ask $3,500 instead of $3,000—cutting the dealer's own consignment profit—then made successive $200 reduction requests. After the $3,500 anchor was set, each $200 nick seemed small.
For store operators: when a vendor, agency or platform recommends against their short-term interest, still check the full economics before accepting later upsells.
When writing upsell copy, an honest minor caveat can build credibility—but only state a real limitation, not a manufactured one.
caveats: The waiter and consignment examples are from the source's fieldwork and a reader anecdote, not controlled ecommerce studies.
Feigned self-criticism is a manipulation tactic in the source; used deceptively it can damage trust once discovered.

cards.title: Apply the Precious-Error Defense to Product Claims and Specs
cards.summary: Because authority pressure makes people stop thinking once a legitimate authority has spoken, errors and misleading claims can pass unchallenged through store operations.
cards.use_when: Reviewing product listings, subscription terms, dosages, compatibility claims or return policies before publishing.
steps: The medicine example shows the hazard: a prescription abbreviated to 'place in R ear' led a nurse to put drops in the patient's anus—nobody questioned it because the doctor had spoken.
Cialdini cites a hospital medication error rate of 12% daily and a Harvard study attributing 10% of cardiac arrests to medication errors.
Run an independent second check on any claim or instruction that comes from a single authoritative source—a supplier spec sheet, a founder's assertion, or a product manual.
Design the check as two independent professional intelligences, as the hospital researchers framed it; do not let a single person both originate and approve a risky claim.
For ecommerce: have someone other than the listing author verify dosage, compatibility, safety and regulatory claims before they go live.
caveats: The medical error statistics are from the source's cited studies from the 1980s and 1990s; they are examples, not current benchmarks.
This is a risk-control practice, not a proven conversion tactic.

cards.title: Expect Underestimated Authority Effects in Customer Research
cards.summary: People consistently misjudge how much authority cues will influence them, so self-reported intent underestimates real compliance.
cards.use_when: Interpreting survey or concept-test feedback on authority-based design (expert endorsements, uniforms, premium branding) or deciding whether to A/B test instead.
steps: Cialdini reports repeated mismatches: in the guard-uniform experiment, students estimated 63% compliance versus the actual 92%; in the luxury-car horn study, students underestimated how long they would wait.
In Bickman's study, college students accurately estimated attitudes toward the street-clothes request but underestimated compliance in the uniform condition.
Treat stated preferences about expert endorsements, professional design or luxury cues as weak evidence—people cannot reliably predict their own reaction.
Run behavioral experiments (A/B tests) where possible, and interpret them against observed behavior rather than survey intent.
When stakeholders insist a design change 'won't matter', point to the systematic underestimation pattern as a reason to test.
caveats: The studies cited are street and small-scale lab studies, not ecommerce experiments.
Underestimation applies to authority cues specifically; it does not justify ignoring all survey data.

cards.title: Commit-First Ordering: Ask for the Lift Before Suggesting It
cards.summary: A large party's server secured an order by requesting commitment when the item looked least available, then upsold from the credibility gained.
cards.use_when: Designing upsell, bundle or add-on flows in cart and checkout.
steps: Cialdini's waiter Vincent allowed guests to order, then recommended cheaper dishes and appeared knowledgeable and honest.
Only after that credibility was established did he suggest costly wines and desserts. Cialdini reports that guests assented and that many who would have skipped dessert ordered it.
The ecommerce adaptation: after resolving a genuine concern for the customer, offer complementary high-margin add-ons—an accessible, verifiable suggestion first, then the higher-priced item.
Avoid starting with the costly add-on; the sequence matters because credibility is earned on the small, disinterested recommendation first.
Test with a single add-on step before stacking multiple upsells, and measure incremental value against margin.
caveats: This draws on the source's restaurant fieldwork and its version of reciprocal obligation and credible authority; ecommerce transfer is a hypothesis.
This draws on the waiter's anecdote, not ecommerce data; the transfer is a hypothesis to test.
If the early recommendation looks insincere, the later upsell will read as a con.

cards.title: Establish a Verification Habit Against Authority Shortcuts
cards.summary: Since authority prompts click-whirr compliance, embed lightweight verification steps rather than relying on vigilance in the moment.
cards.use_when: Setting store operations for supplier approvals, pricing decisions, creative review or claims sign-off.
steps: Cialdini argues the protective tactic is to remove the element of surprise by understanding how easily authority symbols are faked.
Build a two-question gate into decisions: is the authority truly an expert on this, and how truthful can we expect them to be here? Apply to both external claims and internal ones.
Focus attention on credentials and their relevance, not on garments, titles or props.
Rotate reviewers so no single 'boss' input bypasses scrutiny, addressing the nonfunctioning second intelligence described in the hospital study.
Document the check so approvals are repeatable rather than depending on individual vigilance.
caveats: Cialdini notes we should not resist authority most of the time; over-applying the check wastes effort on sound expert advice.
The hospital and con-artist cases are illustrative extremes, not store benchmarks.

has to do, he says, with a deep-seated sense of duty to authority within us all. According to Milgram, the real culprit in the experiments was his subject’s inability to defy the wishes of the boss of the study—the lab-coated researcher who urged and, if need be, directed the subjects to perform their duties, despite the emotional and physical mayhem they were causing. The evidence supporting Milgram’s obedience to authority explanation is strong. First, it is clear that, without the researcher’s directives to continue, the subjects would have ended the experiment quickly. They hated what they were doing and agonized over their victim’s 160 / Influence agony. They implored the researcher to let them stop. When he refused, they went on, but in the process they trembled, they perspired, they shook, they stammered protests and additional pleas for the victim’s release. Their fingernails dug into their own flesh; they bit their lips until they bled; they held their heads in their hands; some fell into fits of uncontrollable nervous laughter. As one outside observer to the experiment wrote: I observed a mature and initially poised businessman enter the laboratory smiling and confident.

 Within twenty minutes he was reduced to a twitching, stuttering wreck who was rapidly approaching a point of nervous collapse. He constantly pulled on his earlobe and twisted his hands. At one point he pushed his fist into his forehead and muttered: “Oh, God, let’s stop it.” And yet he continued to respond to every word of the experimenter and obeyed to the end.1 In addition to these observations, Milgram has provided even more convincing evidence for the obedience-to-authority interpretation of his subjects’ behavior. In a later study, for instance, he had the researcher and the victim switch scripts so that the researcher told the Teacher to stop delivering shocks to the victim, while the victim insisted bravely that the Teacher continue. The result couldn’t have been clearer; 100 percent of the subjects refused to give one additional shock when it was merely the fellow subject who demanded it. The identical finding appeared in another version of the experiment in which the researcher and fellow subject switched roles so that it was the researcher who was strapped into the chair and the fellow subject who ordered the Teacher to continue—over the protests of the researcher. Again, not one subject touched another shock lever. The extreme degree to which subjects in Milgram’s situation were attentive to the wishes of authority was documented in yet another variation of the basic study. In this case, Milgram presented the Teacher with two researchers, who issued contradictory orders; one ordered the Teacher to terminate the shocks when the victim cried out for release, while the other maintained that the experiment should go on. These conflicting instructions reliably produced what may have been the project’s only humor: In tragicomic befuddlement and with eyes darting from one researcher to another, subjects would beseech the pair to agree on a single command they could follow: “Wait, wait. Which is it going to be? One says stop, one says go. Which is it!?” When the researchers remained at loggerheads, the subjects tried frantically to determine who was the bigger boss. Failing this route to obedience with the authority, every subject finally followed his better instincts and Robert B. Cialdini Ph.D / 161 ended the shocks. Not only does it work forcefully on us, but it also does so unexpectedly. HOW TO SAY NO One protective tactic we can use against authority status is to remove its element of surprise. Because we typically misperceive the profound impact of authority (and its symbols) on our actions, we are at the disadvantage of being insufficiently cautious about its presence in compliance situations. A fundamental form of defense against this problem, therefore, is a heightened awareness of authority power. When this awareness is coupled with a recognition of how easily authority symbols can be faked, the benefit will be a properly guarded approach to situations involving authority-influence attempts. Should the patron be dining alone, Vincent selected a friendly demeanor—cordial, conversational, and warm. But Vincent reserved the trick of seeming to argue against his own interests for large parties of eight to twelve people. Here his technique was veined with genius. When it was time for the first person, normally a lady, to order, he went into his act. No matter what she selected, Vincent reacted identically: His brow furrowed, his hand hovered above his order pad, and after looking quickly over his shoulder for the manager, he leaned conspiratorially toward the table to report for all to hear, “I’m afraid that is not as good tonight as it normally is. Might I recommend instead the____or the____?” (Here Vincent suggested a pair of menu items that were fifty cents or so less expensive than the dish the patron had selected initially.) “They are both excellent tonight.” With this single maneuver, Vincent engaged several important principles of influence. First, even those who did not take his suggestions felt that Vincent had done them a favor by offering valuable information to help them order. Everyone felt grateful, and consequently the rule for reciprocity would work in his favor when it came time to decide on his gratuity. But besides hiking the percentage of his tip, Vincent’s maneuver also placed him in a favorable position to increase the size of the table’s order. It established him as an authority on the current stores of the house; he clearly knew what was and wasn’t good that night. Moreover—and this is where seeming to argue against his own interests came in—it proved him to be a trustworthy informant, because he recommended dishes that were slightly less expensive than originally ordered. Rather than trying to line his own pockets, he seemed to have the customers’ best interests at heart. To all appearances, he was at once knowledgeable and honest, a combination that gave him great credibility. And Vincent was quick to exploit the advantage of this credible image. Cialdini Ph.D / 175 ished giving their food orders, he would say, “Very well, and would you like me to suggest or select some wine to go with your meals?” As I watched the scene repeated almost nightly, there was a notable consistency to the customers’ reactions—smiles, nods, and for the most part, general assent. Even from the distance of my vantage point, one could read their thoughts from their faces. “Sure,” they seemed to say, “you know what’s good here, and you’re obviously on our side. Tell us what to get.” Looking pleased, Vincent, who did know his vintages, would respond with some excellent (and costly) choices. He was similarly persuasive when it came time for dessert decisions. Patrons who otherwise would have passed up the dessert course or shared with a friend were swayed to partake fully by Vincent’s rapturous descriptions of the Baked Alaska and chocolate mousse. Who, after all, is more believable than a demonstrated expert of proven sincerity? By combining the factors of reciprocity and credible authority into a single, elegant maneuver, Vincent was able to inflate substantially both the percentage of his tip and the base charge on which it was figured. His proceeds from this trick were handsome, indeed. But notice that much of his profit came from an apparent lack of concern for personal profit. Seeming to argue against his financial interests served those interests extremely well. READER’S REPORT From a Young Businessman “About two years ago, I was trying to sell my old car because I’d already bought a new one. One day I passed a used-car lot with a sign reading, WE WILL SELL YOUR CAR FOR MORE. Just what I wanted, I thought; so I stopped in to talk with the owner. I told him I wanted to get about three thousand dollars for my old car, and he said he thought I should be asking for a lot more because it was worth at least thirty-five-hundred dollars. CHESTERTON T HE CITY OF MESA, ARIZONA, IS A SUBURB IN THE PHOENIX AREA where I live. Perhaps the most notable features of Mesa are its sizable Mormon population—next to that of Salt Lake City, the largest in the world—and a huge Mormon temple located on exquisitely kept grounds in the center of the city. Although I had appreciated the landscaping and architecture from a distance, I had never been interested enough in the temple to go inside until the day I read a newspaper article that told of a special inner sector of Mormon temples to which no one has access but faithful members of the Church. Even potential converts must not see it. There is one exception to the rule, however. For a few days immediately after a temple is newly constructed, nonmembers are allowed to tour the entire structure, including the otherwise restricted section. The newspaper story reported that the Mesa temple had recently been refurbished and that the renovations had been extensive enough to classify it as “new” by Church standards. Thus, for the next several days only, non-Mormon visitors could see the temple area traditionally banned to them. I remember quite well the effect of the article on me: I immediately resolved to take a tour. But when I phoned a friend to ask if he wanted to come along, I came to understand something that changed my decision just as quickly. After declining the invitation, my friend wondered why I seemed so intent on a visit. I was forced to admit that, no, I had never been inclined toward the idea of a temple tour before, that I had no questions about the Mormon religion I wanted answered, that I had no general interest in the architecture of houses of worship, and that I expected to find nothing more spectacular or stirring than I might see at a number of other temples, churches, or cathedrals in the area. It became clear as I spoke that the special lure of the temple had a sole cause: If I did not experience the restricted sector shortly, I would never again have the chance. Something that, on its own merits, held little appeal for me had become decidedly more attractive merely because it would soon become unavailable. Since that encounter with the scarcity principle—that opportunities seem more valuable to us when their availability is limited—I have begun to notice its influence over a whole range of my actions. For instance, I routinely will interrupt an interesting face-to-face conversation to answer the ring of an unknown caller. In such a situation, the caller has a compelling feature that my face-to-face partner does not: potential unavailability. If I don’t take the call, I might miss it (and the information it carries) for good. Never mind that the ongoing conversation may be highly engaging or important—much more than I could reasonably expect an average phone call to be. With each unanswered ring, the phone interaction becomes less retrievable. For that reason and for that moment, I want it more than the other. The idea of potential loss plays a large role in human decision making. In fact, people seem to be more motivated by the thought of losing something than by the thought of gaining something of equal value. For instance, homeowners told how much money they could lose from inadequate insulation are more likely to insulate their homes than those told how much money they could save. Similar results have been obtained by health researchers: Pamphlets urging young women to check for breast cancer through self-examinations are significantly more successful if they state their case in terms of what stands to be lost (e.g., “You can lose several potential health benefits by failing to spend only five minutes each month doing breast self-examination”) rather than gained (e.g., “You can gain several potential health benefits by spending only five minutes each month doing breast self-examination”).1 Collectors of everything from baseball cards to antiques are keenly aware of the influence of the scarcity principle in determining the worth of an item. As a rule, if it is rare or becoming rare, it is more valuable. Especially enlightening as to the importance of scarcity in the collectibles market is the phenomenon of the “precious mistake.” Flawed items—a blurred stamp or a double-struck coin—are sometimes the most valued Robert B. Cialdini Ph.D / 179 of all. Thus a stamp carrying a three-eyed likeness of George Washington is anatomically incorrect, aesthetically unappealing, and yet highly sought after. There is instructive irony here: Imperfections that would otherwise make for rubbish make for prized possessions when they bring along an abiding scarcity. With the scarcity principle operating so powerfully on the worth we assign things, it is natural that compliance professionals will do some related operating of their own. Probably the most straightforward use of the scarcity principle occurs in the “limited-number” tactic, when the customer is informed that a certain product is in short supply that cannot be guaranteed to last long. During the time I was researching compliance strategies by infiltrating various organizations, I saw the limited-number tactic employed repeatedly in a range of situations: “There aren’t more than five convertibles with this engine left in the state. And when they’re gone, that’s it, ’cause we’re not making ’em anymore.” “This is one of only two unsold corner lots in the entire development. You wouldn’t want the other one; it’s got a nasty east-west exposure.” “You may want to think seriously about buying more than one case today because production is backed way up and there’s no telling when we’ll get any more in.” Sometimes the limited-number information was true, sometimes it was wholly false. But in each instance, the intent was to convince customers of an item’s scarcity and thereby increase its immediate value in their eyes. I admit to developing a grudging admiration for the practitioners who made this simple device work in a multitude of ways and styles. I was most impressed, however, with a particular version that extended the basic approach to its logical extreme by selling a piece of merchandise at its scarcest point—when it seemingly could no longer be had. The tactic was played to perfection in one appliance store I investigated, where 30 to 50 percent of the stock was regularly listed as on sale. Suppose a couple in the store seemed from a distance to be moderately interested in a certain sale item. There are all sorts of cues that tip off such interest—closer-than-normal examination of the appliance, a casual look at any instruction booklets associated with the appliance, discussions held in front of the appliance, but no attempt to seek out a salesperson for further information. After observing the couple so engaged, a salesperson might approach and say, “I see you’re interested in this model here, and I can understand why; it’s a great machine at a great price. But, unfortunately, I sold it to another couple not more than twenty minutes ago. And, if I’m not mistaken, it was the last one we had.” The customers’ disappointment registers unmistakably. Because of its lost availability, the appliance jumps suddenly in attractiveness. 180 / Influence Typically, one of the customers asks if there is any chance that an unsold model still exists in the store’s back room, warehouse, or other location. “Well,” the salesperson allows, “that is possible, and I’d be willing to check. But do I understand that this is the model you want and if I can get it for you at this price, you’ll take it?” Therein lies the beauty of the technique. In accord with the scarcity principle, the customers are asked to commit to buying the appliance when it looks least available—and therefore most desirable. Many customers do agree to a purchase at this singularly vulnerable time. Thus, when the salesperson (invariably) returns with the news that an additional supply of the appliance has been found, it is also with a pen and sales contract in hand. The information that the desired model is in good supply may actually make some customers find it less attractive again.2 But by then, the business transaction has progressed too far for most people to renege. The purchase decision made and committed to publicly at an earlier, crucial point still holds. They buy. Related to the limited-number technique is the “deadline” tactic, in which some official time limit is placed on the customer’s opportunity to get what the compliance professional is offering. Much like my experience with the Mormon temple’s inner sanctum, people frequently find themselves doing what they wouldn’t particularly care to do simply because the time to do so is shrinking. The adept merchandiser makes this tendency pay off by arranging and publicizing customer deadlines—witness the collage of such newspaper ads in Figure 7–3—that generate interest where none may have existed before. Concentrated instances of this approach often occur in movie advertising.
